articles.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
articles.summary: The Nvidia scandal has raised questions over whether advanced AI chips ended up in China, despite US restrictions.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley as well as the political establishment By Dearbail Jordan ,  Business reporter   and   Lily Jamali ,  North America Technology correspondent ,  Reporting from Palo Alto, CA 
- Published 15 November 2026 
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says. 
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees. 
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions. 
The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business. 
Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence". 
It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". 
Also on Sunday, US Congressman John Moolenaar said that Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Select Committee on China, which he chairs, as well as the House Foreign Affairs and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. 
The committee heads had threatened to issue subpoenas to Huang if he did not comply with their requests to testify. 
Moolenaar told CBS, BBC's US partner, that none were ultimately issued. Huang's testimony is expected to take place behind close doors, with the dates still being finalised. 
"That's going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, and to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia's philosophy and may have had an influence on some of our policies with respect to AI and export controls," the congressman told the Face The Nation programme. 
Separately, a group of tech leaders, including Space X's Elon Musk, have been trying to rally support to have Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO. 
A representative for Huang declined to comment on a report in the Financial Times Sunday suggesting that he was discussing a comeback to the firm he co-founded. 
On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips. 
Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process". 
The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals. 
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips. 
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang. 
Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? 
Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced chips to China. 
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls. 
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations. 
Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate". 
China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

articles.title: What we know as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns over affair allegations
articles.summary: The billionaire tech executive has left the company following reports of a second extramarital affair.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
Watch: What we know so far about Nvidia CEO resignation By Lily Jamali ,  North America Technology correspondent   and   Peter Hoskins ,  Business reporter 
- Published 9 November 2026 Updated 12 November 2026 
One of the AI industry's most important figures has resigned amid allegations that he had extramarital affairs with two women - one a suspected Chinese spy and the other a company executive. 
Chip-maker Nvidia hired a major law firm earlier this week to investigate CEO Jensen Huang's reported relationship with a woman who was allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset. 
Now he has resigned after its stocks plummeted on Wednesday following US media reports about a second alleged affair. 
Huang admitted , external earlier this week to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and he apologised for hurting her and their children. 
Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters. 
- 
Nvidia stocks plummet in US after CEO Jensen Huang quits in wake of affair with suspected Chinese spy 
How was Huang removed? 
Nvidia's board met on Wednesday evening to decide whether its CEO should remain with the company. 
It had 11 directors on its board, including Huang. The firm's CEO could be removed with or without cause by a majority vote of directors. 
But that wasn't in the end needed - the board instead announced Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member. 
It thanked him for his "immeasurable contributions" to Nvidia, which it said were "profound". 
There was no mention of the accusations of adultery. 
Who will replace him? 
Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO . 
It is less clear is who will replace Huang on a permanent basis. 
One possibility is Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky. He has been at the company as long as Huang, and for years led its product engineering work. 
Huang's children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez also work at Nvidia in senior roles, but they are relatively young and inexperienced. 
And there is also the option of Ian Buck, who runs high-performance computing at the firm. He developed the technology which allowed graphics cards to be used for other computing tasks, which enabled Nvidia to capitalise on the growth of AI. 
What we know about Huang's affairs 
A New York Times report at the weekend revealed Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who US intelligence officials believed was a spy for Beijing. 
She had previously been photographed with him on several occasions. 
The tech giant's board of directors launched an independent external investigation on Sunday following the reports. They earlier said Huang's interactions with the woman were "not unusual or unexpected". 
Then on Wednesday, the New York Times reported Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him. 
She did not respond to the BBC's request for comment. 
Image source, AFP Image caption, 
Jensen Huang (left) and Alice Huang - also known as Huang Le - at an event 
Who is Jensen Huang? 
Born in Taiwan in 1963, Jensen Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the west coast of the US. 
He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University. 
He worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. 
Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" , he has a reputation as a workaholic with incredibly high standards for his staff. 
He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. 
"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on the Jensen Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today. 
The Nvidia co-founder has a famously close relationship with US President Donald Trump. 
At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang. 
Figure caption, 
Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? 
Who is Alice Huang? 
US officials believed Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported , external . 
She was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. 
Her company had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, which the firm said had been investigated and debunked. 
However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singaporean government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. 
The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment. 
It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing. 
When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not. 
China has rejected the spying allegations as "entirely groundless". 
-

- Published 5 days ago 
- 
Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond 
- Published 6 days ago 
- 
Nvidia hires major New York law firm to investigate Jensen Huang affair 
- Published 5 days ago 
Why does it matter? 
Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world - so the slump in its value which followed Huang's resignation hits investors large and small. 
The firm is also at the heart of US and China's AI race , which is why the billionaire's affair has sparked national security fears among US lawmakers. 
Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the concern is if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities. 
The US advantage is in large part because of companies like Nvidia, working with producers such as the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips. 
Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security. 
This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Huang once saying Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. 
He has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way. 
The revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China . 
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
Nvidia boss Jensen Huang and US President Donald Trump at the White House 
What investigations are now under way? 
After news broke out about the first affair, Nvidia launched an independent investigation and hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. 
It will be led by Joon Kim, a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District who is now a litigation partner at the law firm. 
US President Donald Trump said the FBI was investigating the scandal, adding that Huang told him he had been unaware the woman he was with was a spy. 
Huang has also been asked to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees on 18 November, but has yet to say he will comply. 
What is Nvidia and how important is it? 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
There is no clear successor for Jensen Huang at Nvidia 
Founded by Huang and fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993, the company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for gaming. 
Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates . 
Huang rescued Nvidia from bankruptcy on more than one occasion, and took risks on AI a long time before the rest of the world did, effectively building the infrastructure from scratch. 
He bet on AI at a time when "there were no customers for the stuff he was building", Witt told the BBC. 
Every notable tech company building AI tools and infrastructure like Amazon, Google and Microsoft now use Nvidia chips. 
Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world. 
Who is Jensen Huang's wife? 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Lori Huang and her husband at a state dinner by Trump for his Chinese President Xi Jinping 
Jensen Huang met his future wife Lori Mills at Oregon State University while studying electrical engineering in the early 1980s. The pair were lab partners. 
They married in 1985 and have two children, Madison and Spencer. 
Earlier this week, Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. 
In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation. The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn. 
Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University. 
Witt told the BBC that Jensen Huang has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, adding: "That's very important to him." 
"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. 
"But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad." 
Additional reporting by Tom McArthur in London, Ayeshea Perera and Tessa Wong in Singapore and Helen Davidson in Sydney

articles.title: Is India rethinking its short-term military recruitment scheme?
articles.summary: India has softened its recruitment scheme, giving young soldiers a longer military stint and another shot at permanent service.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
There are currently 300,000 Agniveers serving in India's defence forces By Nikita Yadav BBC News, Delhi 
- Published 54 minutes ago 
For generations of young Indians, joining the armed forces offered something few other jobs did - a steady career, financial security, the promise of a pension after retirement and the pride of serving their country. 
In 2022, the government upended that arrangement, announcing a new reform scheme under which young men and women entering the military would serve for just four years. Only a quarter would be allowed to stay on permanently. The rest would return to civilian life with a lump-sum payment, but without the pension and other benefits that had long made military service an attractive career. 
Now, as the first batch of recruits prepares to complete its four-year term, the government is offering them a chance to stay longer, in a significant shift in a policy that has been fiercely debated since its introduction. 
On 4 November, Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani announced that recruits who failed to secure permanent positions under the Agnipath, or "path of fire", programme would be offered another two years of service at higher pay. They would then get a second opportunity to join the regular forces, provided they met the selection criteria. 
Gen Subramani said the decision followed feedback from the forces and insisted that Agnipath would continue. 
But the timing is significant. More than 18,300 recruits from the first batch are due to complete their initial tenure by the end of 2026. Officials say the new arrangement will be offered to more than 300,000 Agniveers - as recruits under the scheme are known - currently serving across the army, navy and air force. 
Whether future batches will also be covered remains unclear. The BBC has contacted the defence ministry for clarification. 
The ministry has defended , external Agnipath, saying internal assessments found the recruits to be physically fit, motivated and technologically adaptable. It also said the scheme had widened recruitment across districts and made the process more standardised. 
But the extension has brought renewed attention to the trade-offs at the heart of the policy - and whether its original ambitions were realistic. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Those selected are trained for months before being inducted into regiments 
When the government introduced Agnipath, it argued the scheme would reduce the average age of the armed forces, lower long-term salary and pension costs and create a younger, more technologically adaptable fighting force. 
But military experts and opposition leaders have questioned whether a four-year contract could replace what had traditionally been a coveted, long-term career in the armed forces. 
"Being a soldier in the armed forces was a chance for these young men to make a life for themselves, to get their families out of poor or lower-middle-income conditions," says retired Maj Gen Yash Mor, a vocal critic of the scheme. 
These concerns were also amplified by the timing of Agnipath's launch. Recruitment had been suspended for nearly two years during the Covid pandemic, leaving thousands of aspirants waiting for vacancies to reopen. 
The changes were greeted by massive protests across the country, with many saying the career path they had spent years preparing for had fundamentally changed. 
This sentiment was felt most in states and cities that have traditionally been major recruitment hubs, where military service has been a family tradition for generations. 
Kulbeer Singh Chaudhary, who runs a recruitment training institute in Dehradun city, says interest in joining the armed forces fell sharply and he stopped conducting Agniveer training batches. 
The latest announcement, he hopes, would reverse that trend. 
"The possibility of a longer engagement and eventual absorption into the forces may offer young candidates greater assurance," he says. 
The changes also come at a time when the armed forces are facing personnel shortages. In November last year, The Indian Express reported , external that the army alone faced a shortfall of nearly 180,000 soldiers and was considering increasing recruitment. 
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
Many young men from small towns spend months preparing for the selection process to join the defence forces 
But the debate over Agnipath goes beyond what happens to recruits after four years. Critics also question whether that is enough time to turn them into experienced soldiers. 
Sanjiv Krishan Sood, a former additional director general of the Border Security Force, has argued , external that the shorter training period is particularly problematic for technical roles requiring specialised skills. 
Retired Maj Gen Mor says military effectiveness depends on experience and trust built over years. 
"It takes eight-to-nine years to turn a raw recruit into a dependable, seasoned soldier - someone capable of handling a tank crew, an artillery gun crew or a small detachment," he says. 
"Over those years, a soldier develops the ethos, camaraderie, brotherhood and fighting spirit that bind a unit together. These qualities cannot be built overnight." 
Sood says the additional two years could help improve recruits' skills, particularly in handling specialised equipment. 
Senior military leaders have also welcomed the extension. Air Vice Marshal Shekhar Yadav told news agency ANI , external it would allow the forces to retain trained personnel for longer. 
But the change could create fresh challenges within military units. 
Regular soldiers, Agniveers on four-year contracts and those serving an additional two years could find themselves working alongside one another despite differences in pay, promotion prospects and post-service benefits. 
Experts warn that these disparities could affect unit cohesion. 
Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, 
Indian soldiers are deployed through the year at the country's borders with China and Pakistan 
There is also the question of whether the changes will undermine one of the government's central objectives: reducing spending. Almost half of India's defence budget , external goes towards salaries and pensions, leaving less money for modernisation and new equipment. 
By limiting the number of personnel eligible for long-term benefits, Agnipath was expected to ease that burden. But critics argue that savings should not come at the expense of military effectiveness. 
"We are not against making changes, but there are ways and means to go about it," says Mor, adding that the government could instead reduce annual recruitment while retaining soldiers for longer periods. 
He also points to India's tense borders with Pakistan and China, where troops remain deployed year-round, placing sustained demands on manpower and operational experience. 
Retired Major-General Birender Singh Dhanoa, meanwhile, questions whether shorter service makes financial sense when the military is investing in training to operate increasingly sophisticated equipment. 
"The amount of time it takes to train, and the financial outlay for training, is much higher for modern equipment. So shouldn't you get the best bang for your buck?" he asks. 
Many retired officers had proposed a different approach when the scheme was announced, he says. 
"We suggested that if you want to reduce your financial burden, you increase the terms and conditions of service. Take these guys for eight-or-nine years and retain a larger number after that." 
The announcement also comes at a politically sensitive time. Elections are due soon in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand - states that have traditionally supplied large numbers of soldiers and where military recruitment remains an important source of employment. 
The opposition Congress party has called the revision a "u-turn", alleging that the government is responding to fears of losing votes. 
For young recruits approaching the end of their contracts, the changes offer some reassurance, but few guarantees. Two more years of service could mean more money, greater experience and another chance at a permanent career. 
But for many, it also means putting their futures on hold, without knowing whether they will eventually be allowed to stay.

articles.title: Clothing factories shut in Bangladesh as workers strike over pay
articles.summary: Workers are striking over demands for a minimum wage of 30,000 taka (£182) a month.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Protesters in Dhaka, Bangladesh, on Friday demanding a new minimum wage By Dan Sales 
- Published 15 November 2026 Updated 31 minutes ago 
Dozens of factories in Bangladesh's main clothes-producing area have been shut by workers striking over a higher minimum wage. 
Nearly 150 sites across the country have been closed in the textile hubs of Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur this weekend. 
The garment industry is big business for Bangladesh, generating nearly $40bn (£30bn) in exports every year and making up 10% of the country's total GDP. 
Workers are striking over demands for a minimum wage of 30,000 taka (£182) a month. The minimum monthly wage in Bangladesh is currently 12,500 taka but employees say this is not enough to deal with the cost of living crisis. 
On Sunday morning workers massed on the Dhaka-Tangail highway in Gazipur to block the road. Traffic was stopped by the protests for about an hour before police stepped in. 
A "No Work No Pay" provision of labour laws allows owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted. 
Police Supt Mohammad Amjad Hossain told the BBC officers shut factories in the city after the workers walked out. 
He said 13 factories were closed on Saturday night and "sixteen factories were closed during the morning unrest". 
- 
Wage protests force hundreds of Bangladesh garment factories to close 
- Published 3 November 
The garment industry in Bangladesh employs about four million workers making clothes for big brands including H&M, Primark and Zara. 
Bangladesh is the world's second largest exporter of ready- to-wear clothes after China and it is feared that the current unrest could have a knock-on effect for international buyers if it carries on for substantial amount of time. 
The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) is calling for protection for factories. 
"BGMEA and BKMEA have questioned the justification of continuing to participate in wage board negotiations without any assurance that the factories will be protected," BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan said. 
"Garment factories that have been unable to continue production due to the ongoing unrest will remain indefinitely closed from tomorrow under... Bangladesh's labour law." 
But critics say workers are being sacrificed for factories to churn out products at competitive prices. 
Joly Talukder, the vice president of the Garment Workers Trade Union Centre, told BBC's Newshour that "workers have carried the costs for years" while factory owners and global retailers profit from their exploitation. 
"They are asking for a wage they can survive on. How can any person of conscience stand against such a basic human demand?" she said. 
On 1 November the government formed a minimum wage board to recommend a revised pay structure for workers. 
The board, chaired by a senior district judge, said at its first meeting it would finalise any recommendations by the end of November. 
Once it is put in place, the revised pay structure is expected to take effect from 1 December.

articles.title: How the Jensen Huang scandal created a headache for business-friendly Singapore
articles.summary: The scandal has cast a spotlight on Singapore's success as a chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images By Tessa Wong   and   Osmond Chia ,  Reporting from Singapore 
- Published 13 November 2026 
A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade. 
On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips. 
For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets. 
With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years. 
Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns. 
But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere. 
Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips. 
Megaspeed is a case in point. 
It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. 
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls. 
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations. 
The city-state has had some success in policing this. 
It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places. 
They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties. 
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Megaspeed's office in Singapore 
In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore. 
The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere. 
Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed. 
But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department. 
Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud. 
In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months. 
Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case. 
Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing. 
In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times. 
Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses. 
Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity. 
On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". 
China has also long rebuffed accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday following a board meeting 
How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness. 
In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively. 
For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law. 
But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities. 
Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case. 
BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road. 
In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed. 
Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man. 
During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS. 
Even after she transferred Megaspeed, C4ADS assessed that she was still "practically in control" of the company, based on her links to Megaspeed via another company as well as LinkedIn posts where she continued to identify herself as Megaspeed's "chairwoman" at conferences. 
Megaspeed has not answered BBC queries regarding the company's and Alice Huang's links to China and the Chinese government. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Alice Huang, seen here in Taipei with Jensen Huang last year, ran Megaspeed for several months in 2023 
All this reinforces the dilemma faced by Singapore. 
"For the longest time, Singapore has managed to enjoy the best of both worlds with excellent relations with US and China," Nanyang Technological University politics and international studies lecturer Dylan Loh said. 
Singapore has long positioned itself as a neutral party between the two superpowers. Its prime minister Lawrence Wong has insisted that his country is neither pro-China nor pro-America, but "pro-Singapore". 
But Loh says this balancing act "has now fast become very difficult to manage and sometimes quite fraught too" with the US-China dispute over chips. 
With the Megaspeed case, the tightrope Singapore has walked is set to get even narrower, according to analysts. 
Beijing may ask why Singapore is investigating issues pertaining to US restrictions and whether they are siding with the US' interests, says Chong Ja Ian, a Singaporean political scientist and non-resident scholar with Carnegie China. 
Washington, in turn, might read Singapore's latest statement as "pushing blame" on the US, which could lead to backlash from the White House, he said. 
"Singapore has made a policy position not to take sides. But by not choosing a side, they run the risk of being seen as complicit" in either side's agenda, he said. 
But Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and China expert at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that this was "not the first or last time Singapore will be caught between the US and China". 
"This is the price that an open economy has to grapple with - you get caught in the middle when things turn sour." 
Additional reporting by Jack Lau of the BBC's Global China Unit.

articles.title: Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a future after Putin
articles.summary: Some Russian tycoons are pining after a return to a 1990s system of oligarchy, when businessmen enjoyed power
articles.full_text:
By Vitaly Shevchenko Chief Analyst, BBC Monitoring 
Hours after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Vladimir Putin gathered Russia's richest men in the Kremlin's cavernous Yekaterininsky Hall. 
More than three dozen of them sat huddled along a wall, wearing face masks because of the Covid pandemic. One Russian newspaper reporter described them as "pale and sleep-deprived". On entering, Putin sat down at the opposite side of the hall, creating a vast space between him and the businessmen. As usual, he was wearing no mask. 
Using his typically coded language, he said he expected them to support the war. 
"I would like to call on you to show understanding of what is going on," he said, "and work together with the government to find the tools which would support production, the economy, jobs." 
In the Kremlin-published video of the meeting, none of the invited billionaires said a word. 
That silence has become a feature of the Russian super-rich. Over the decades of Putin's rule, they have learnt that the price of piping up could be high. In 2003, oil magnate Mikhail Khodorkovsky, Russia's richest man at the time, who was funding a number of opposition groups, accused Putin of presiding over rampant corruption. He spent the next 10 years behind bars, convicted of tax evasion, fraud and embezzlement - a warning to other would-be critics. He denied the charges. 
Image source, ALEXEY NIKOLSKY/SPUTNIK/AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
The silence of Russian businessmen at a Kremlin summit with Putin in 2022 perhaps demonstrated their fear of the president 
And even if any of the tycoons objected to the war, they have tended to keep their thoughts to themselves. 
But even in that silence, there are murmurings: some members of Russia's once-mighty business elite seem to be imagining a Russia after Putin. They are wondering if, once the president has left office or died, the country might look more like it did in the 1990s, when the oligarchs enjoyed the fruits of power - or even if a healthier politics may take root. 
The journalist Arkady Ostrovsky, a prominent Kremlin-watcher at The Economist newspaper who recently spent hours interviewing one of Russia's richest men, says he feels that a "historic, political shift is happening" in terms of how the ultra-rich view the future of the country. 
Restless tycoons 
The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 gave birth to a new, powerful force on the domestic scene: people who took advantage of the end of communism and became extraordinarily rich, and then wanted to control politicians for their own benefit. They were dubbed "the oligarchs", from Ancient Greek for the "few who rule".  They had money, which back then meant power. 
This era of the "wild 1990s" was when the so-called "new Russians" burst onto the scene. Huge state companies came up for grabs, and men with the right connections became millionaires - even billionaires - almost overnight. Corruption was rife, cronyism rampant, and contract killings frequent. 
But almost immediately after Putin was first elected as president in 2000, he subjugated the oligarchs. He had little interest in sharing power with anyone else. He could afford to stand up to the billionaires because Russia's economy was getting back on its feet, and the central government was getting stronger. 
Image source, NurPhoto/NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, 
Some oligarchs developed a distinctive dress sense in the 1990s, as later satirised by this St Petersburg artist 
Bill Browder, a financier who used to be the biggest foreign investor in Russia, and was banned from the country in 2005 after campaigning against corruption, says the Russian tycoons cowered and wilted in front of Putin - for example at the Davos economic forum, in the pre-war years when they were still welcomed there. 
"I can remember seeing oligarchs walking around like they own the place, the most arrogant and self-confident individuals. And then Putin showed up, and it was just remarkable to see how these supposedly alpha-male-on-steroids individuals turned into absolutely subordinate, almost desperate schoolchildren," he tells the BBC. 
Since the outbreak of war in 2022, the Kremlin has kept Russia's rich businessmen in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick. Critics of the war have seen their assets seized, while loyalists have been rewarded with lavish government war contracts: today there are more Russian billionaires than ever (155 in total, according to Forbes magazine).  Their collective wealth has reached a new high of nearly $700bn (£525bn). 
But even for those tycoons who have stayed loyal and been rewarded, all of that money doesn't seem to be making them happy. Some are growing restless. 
Autocracy, oligarchy or democracy? 
Their billions do not go as far as they used to: domestically, they cannot buy much political influence. 
"They have no cards, they have no game," exiled politician and analyst Dmitry Nekrasov says. "They're rich because they've got something to do with Putin, not the other way round." 
And outside of Russia, they are ostracised because of the Western sanctions imposed on Russia after its full-scale invasion. 
"They're treated like low-level criminals. They can't fly their private jets. Their yachts can't park in all the best harbours in Europe. It must be very awful and humiliating for them," says Browder, the avowed Putin critic. 
And so, quietly, some of their minds are turning to what happens after Putin leaves the scene. That's what I'm told by well-placed analysts, who are immersed in the world of these tycoons. 
There's no immediate prospect of the president's departure, and there's no reason to think he's in bad health. But Putin, who turned 74 last month, has served in the Kremlin for a quarter of a century; people in Moscow know that his exit will come one day. When asked by Reuters last year if he intends to serve until 2036, when his constitutional term technically ends, Putin replied: "Only God knows if we have enough health." 
Image source, CARL DE SOUZA/AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
One prominent oligarch of the 1990s was Boris Berezovsky, who fell out with the Kremlin and lived his later years in the UK 
If Putin resigned or died in office, the prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, would take over. But Mishustin has not exhibited any presidential ambitions (that's probably a key reason he was appointed). That would create something of a power vacuum. 
In that scenario, Russia-watchers I have spoken with envisage a few potential scenarios. 
Some in the West, and no doubt within Russia, hope that democracy might flourish in a post-Putin Russia, with government led by the people, rather than by a new cadre of oligarchs or a single autocrat. But this seems like the least likely path, analysts say. Key democratic institutions have been eroded or destroyed over Putin's rule. "Russia is so used to violence, it has grown unaccustomed to standard democratic procedures," says Alexandra Prokopenko, an exiled Russian journalist and analyst. 
Another path is more autocracy. A different figure could replace Putin and continue his culture of repression. But Prokopenko thinks this wouldn't be another strongman dictatorship - at least not right away. These things take time, she says: at first, Putin's successor would be weaker than him, with fewer resources. 
And then there's the third option: tycoons re-assert their power and Russia returns to something resembling a 1990s-style system of oligarchy. Dmitry Nekrasov, a former Kremlin adviser and opposition politician who now lives in exile, says under this scenario, the country would be governed by a handful of powerful elite clans in alliance with business interests. 
This last option, of course, is the one that many tycoons want. "They'd like to return to a time when they were listened to, when they were not stripped of assets and when they understood the rules of the game," says Prokopenko, who has spent a lot of time speaking to Russia's richest people. 
Though their power has been seriously curtailed since the 1990s, it's still worth listening to the tycoons: given their immense wealth, it seems likely that sooner or later they will try to re-assert their political influence. 
Already, some are "trying to be friends with the right sort of security officials or ministers", says Nekrasov, the exiled politician. But he says any further steps are "too dangerous to take". 
Image source, Vladimir Smirnov SPUTNIK/KREMLIN POOL/EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, 
Putin has kept tycoons in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine 
He says the behaviour of the tycoons in coming years will depend in part on their finances. Those who have lots of liquid cash will be more confident to "play political games" and jockey for position, preparing for a post-Putin country. But those whose wealth is dependent on state contracts or government goodwill will feel too afraid, in case they lose everything, he says. 
Prokopenko says there's already been a shift in how the businessmen talk about Putin. They used to nickname him "Nachalnik" (which translates as "boss"), as well as "Perviy" ("first"), or by his initials "VV" - all nicknames that convey a degree of respect. Now they call him "Ded", with what Prokopenko calls "a pinch of contempt". "Ded" translates as "oldie" or "granddad" - a much less reverent name. 
Some rich Russians are pining after a "return of politics into people's lives", she says, with less repression, more open speech, and healthier competition between parties and politicians. 
But at the moment, she says, they are too afraid to make that happen due to Russia's stifling atmosphere. Prokopenko interviewed one tycoon who physically sat on his phone during the whole conversation, because he thought it would make digital eavesdropping more difficult for secret police. "I thought that it's an absolutely Stalinistic type of fear. It's absolutely irrational," she says. 
A bombshell interview 
An interesting clue for what tycoons might want from a post-Putin future came from Andrey Melnichenko, who is known as the world's fertiliser king and is currently Russia's eighth richest man. 
Earlier this year, he surprised observers by giving an interview to The Economist - a rare thing for a rich Russian to do, especially to a publication from a country the Kremlin considers unfriendly. They also published an essay written by him. 
In parts of the interview, Melnichenko repeated Kremlin talking points. He said that Ukraine is a battlefield between Russia and the West, and he thinks the West ignored Russia's security concerns and threatens its sovereignty. 
But then it got more interesting. Melnichenko did not call for Putin to go, but - and it's a big but - he argued for a change that would bring about an end to one-man rule in Russia. He said Russia needs to engage more with the world. 
Prokopenko thinks the tycoon was trying to stir a public conversation. It was a "call on rich people like him to start talking", she says. 
The journalist who interviewed him, Arkady Ostrovsky, tells me the pair had "tense and heated discussions" in "hotels and cafes, mostly drinking coffee, lots of coffee, sometimes smoking". He says the tycoon seemed to be "genuinely thinking" about his answers, rather than giving politician-style spin. 
Nothing in Russia is simple, and most observers think the interview probably happened with some form of approval - implicit or explicit - from the Kremlin. We don't know why authorities would have been happy to authorise the unusual call for change; it's possible they were trying to show that some degree of pluralism still exists in the country. 
No tycoons came out to support him. Still, the journalist feels that Melnichenko was not speaking for himself alone, but also for his fellow businessmen. 
Image source, Andrey Rudakov/Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
Some tycoons feel ostracised because of Western sanctions, unable to fly private jets and visit Western resorts like Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat in southern France, which used to be popular with rich Russians 
Some of them are hoping that after Putin's departure, the country might become an "oligarchic republic", as journalist Ostrovsky puts it - something like how it looked in the 1990s, with the business elites in charge. 
Based on his years of reporting on Russia, Ostrovsky says that many of the country's mega-rich currently feel a "sense of complete dead end, which this war has led Russia to… [an] absence of the future". 
But even if the tycoons are thinking about the future, there's a slim prospect of them acting any time soon, it seems. 
Browder, the Putin critic, says that although many of them are unhappy, they're unlikely to conspire against Putin while he is still alive. "They understand that if they were to do anything that would challenge Putin, he would kill them. And Putin is a very paranoid little man." 
Mike Calvey, an American financier who used to be a key investor in Russia, agrees. "What can they do besides just go straight to the prison and lose their assets? It's easy for people who are sitting in London to say that, 'why don't you just all go stand up and go straight to prison?' That's really what would happen." 
Russia's richest men used to be able to pull strings at the highest levels of power. Once Putin is gone, there is no doubt they will try to claw back their past influence. The question is: will remnants of the current regime let them?

articles.title: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
articles.summary: Fear and misinformation surrounds the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo - Dr Kamwanga's mother was not immune.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Braton Serge/BBC By Ruth Alonga BBC Africa ,  Reporting from Butembo 
- Published 15 November 2026 
When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified. 
They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there. 
"Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him. 
But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive. 
This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded. 
Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry. 
Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community. 
After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience. 
"As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works. 
The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate. 
Image source, Braton Serge/BBC Image caption, 
Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga uses his book to help convince sceptics that Ebola is real 
The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team. 
After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve. 
Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north. 
This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance. 
After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea. 
This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre. 
"She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says. 
Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance. 
He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids. 
Image caption, 
Dr Kamwanga's mother says his experience has helped dispel some of the misinformation she had heard about Ebola 
The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. 
"The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea. 
In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding. 
Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified. 
"I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains. 
Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok. 
The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him. 
However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged.

- Published 18 June 
"We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC. 
For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region. 
He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance. 
Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns. 
"We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC. 
They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola. 
Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation. 
After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust. 
"I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact." 
During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real. 
But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding. 
Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says. 
"Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate". 
He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion. 
But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone. 
Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community. 
He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly." 
He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing . 
"The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says. 
The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment. 
Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease. 
"Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."

Elon Musk joins 158,000 others calling for Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang in open letter
Silicon Valley figures back CEO ousted after revelations of affair with suspected Chinese spy, as US treasury secretary urges Nvidia to carry out ‘dramatic shake-up’ 
Elon Musk and a host of other tech executives are among more than 158,000 signatories of an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia chief, days after he resigned from the multi-trillion dollar chip company. 
The letter demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”. 
Huang’s resignation on Thursday ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI giant he co-founded, after revelations he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate. 
US lawmakers from both sides of the aisle have demanded Huang and Nvidia appear before Congress to explain whether US national security had been put at risk – with some in the president’s own party suggesting that Donald Trump’s administration must also must answer questions on what it knew about Huang’s relationship with the suspected Chinese spy. ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick 
Read more 
According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed a possible return to the company with people close to him. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for the former Nvidia ‌chief’s return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House. 
“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person said, adding that the efforts had Huang’s support. 
On Friday, two major shareholders, investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board to keep “all options” open. 
In Washington, however, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent argued on Sunday that Nvidia should look “outside” the company for its next chief. “They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent said on Fox News. 
Bessent also called on Nvidia to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than Huang’s affair with the alleged spy for Beijing. 
The US forbids sales to China of the most cutting-edge AI chips, as parts of its strategy to stay ahead of Beijing in the race to dominate artificial intelligence. 
In late 2025, Trump authorised sales of Nvidia chips called H200s to the Chinese – but not the most advanced chips used to run AI models reshaping modern society. 
“Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese,” Bessent said, adding that it was important to examine “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions”. 
Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang’s behaviour within the next 10 days. 
Alongside Musk, the tech heavyweight signatories on the letter calling for Huang’s return include Tim Sweeney, founder and CEO of video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, president of Y Combinator, San Francisco’s most renowned business incubator. 
Another signatory, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had “erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company”. 
More than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company’s workforce. 
The support illustrates the unique standing of Huang, who is seen as a godfather of AI within the industry. Under his leadership, Nvidia became a pivotal Silicon Valley investor, financing datacentres and startups, earning it the nickname “the central bank of AI”. 
But the company has also faced criticism that it has fuelled a speculative investment bubble. Huang fought any constraints on the AI race, clashing on these issues with Claude creator Anthropic and its chief Dario Amodei. 
Jensen Huang and other Nvidia officials have agreed to testify before Congress, according to officials, but no date has been set yet.

Anthony Albanese welcomes Trump-Xi-Putin summit – even as European leaders express reservations
‘We think dialogue is a good thing,’ Australian PM says after German chancellor urges the US to work with Europe for peace in Ukraine 
Australia has endorsed this week’s historic summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China, even as European leaders warn that the US president must not make major concessions over the war in Ukraine. 
The three-way summit is planned to take place in Shenzhen, where the leaders will gather for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , has warned the talks must not lead to a redistribution of influence among world powers or the abandonment of his country, more than four years into the war sparked by Putin’s full-scale invasion. 
Speaking in Manila on Sunday, the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese , welcomed the talks taking place but insisted the clear message to Putin was that the war should end. 
Albanese, in the Philippines before a meeting of Quad leaders and talks with south-east Asian leaders at the Asean summit, left open the possibility of joining an Apec group photo with Putin if China wished for it to go ahead. 
“We think that dialogue is a good thing and we await the outcome of that dialogue,” he said. Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up?

“It’s obviously quite significant, the fact that President Trump will be at Asean as well as at Apec, and that we’ll have a Quad leaders meeting as well. 
“We want to see something constructive come out of that, including we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts around the world.” 
German’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz , expressed hesitation about the talks at a meeting of EU leaders on Friday. 
“I want to state our message to the US very clearly once again: please, no surprises,” he said. “Stay on Team Europe and Team Ukraine , and let us work together for a genuine peace in Ukraine.” 
France’s president, Emmanuel Macron , warned against forcing “an unjust peace” on Ukraine and, by extension, all of Europe. 
“That is the spirit of defeat,” Macron said. “That is a recipe for another war.” 
The meeting has been compared to a 1945 summit at Yalta , in southern Crimea, when then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin carved up influence across war-ravaged Europe. Zelenskyy has warned that the meeting must not turn into “Yalta 2, 3, 4”. 
The historian Timothy Garton Ash has called the trilateral summit, organised after a proposal by Putin last month, “a sort of parody” of Yalta, even as analysts say decisions on the future of Ukraine or China’s ambitions to take control of Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely. 
Albanese said the summit would not undercut a growing push by countries including Australia and Canada for middle powers to have greater influence in world affairs. 
“We’ll continue to engage with like-minded countries,” he said. “There are two super powers in the world. 
“What’s important about the struggle of the people of Ukraine is that they’re not just standing up for their own sovereignty; they’re standing up for the international rule of law.” 
Asked if he would join the so-called “family photo” of Apec leaders if Putin took part, Albanese said he would consider the wishes of China as the host nation. But he said the Russian president should know Australia’s opposition to the invasion. 
“If he’s in a room where I am, I’m sure they’ll hear my contribution,” Albanese said. 
After the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting, Australia’s Penny Wong joined with European and Canadian counterparts to avoid a group photo . It was cancelled by US officials when a third of participants declined to stand alongside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov. 
Albanese signed a new defence agreement with the Philippines on Sunday, visiting the supply ship HMAS Stalwart in the Port of Manila. Australia is helping to strengthen the Philippines’ defensive capability against Chinese aggression. 
More freedom-of-navigation naval exercises are planned in an attempt to counter Beijing’s efforts to influence the South and East China seas.

View image in fullscreen 
China will have the home advantage as it welcomes Donald Trump and others for the Apec leaders’ meeting in its southern technology hub of Shenzhen. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images 
World leaders head to Asia for back-to-back diplomatic summits
Tussle for influence as trade, tech and regional security to take centre stage in China, Philippines and Cambodia meetings 
World leaders will fly in to Asia for back-to-back high-level summits this week against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US. 
Beijing will have the home advantage when it welcomes Donald Trump to its southern technology hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. It starts two weeks after the US leader lost midterm elections . 
The summit also comes after an awkward-at-best revelation that the head of Nvidia, the US chipmaker that for a long time was the world’s most valuable company, was having an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects was a Chinese spy . 
Apec represents more than 60% of global GDP and has primarily promoted free trade and multilateralism. This year’s meeting could be defined, however, by the confirmed trilateral meeting between Trump, the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia. 
The three-way meeting has been likened to a modern-day Yalta, when in 1945 then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to carve up Europe after the second world war. However, analysts say a “Yalta 2.0” that issues edicts on Ukraine and Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely. 
View image in fullscreen 
Protesters in Manila on Friday object to Donald Trump’s participation in the Asean summit. Photograph: Rolex dela Peña/EPA 
Xiaoyu Pu, an associate professor at the University of Nevada’s department of political science, said a three-way meeting “might be more symbolic than substantive, although symbolism itself matters in great-power diplomacy. 
“Trump appears interested in nuclear arms control and denuclearisation. Xi’s priority is likely to maintain a stable relationship with Washington while preserving China’s strategic partnership with Russia. Putin, meanwhile, wants to maintain his bargaining leverage over Ukraine.” 
Apec begins on Wednesday and follows a flurry of other diplomatic gatherings, chief among them the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) meeting in the Philippines , starting on Sunday, which Trump will attend. 
View image in fullscreen 
A poster in Siem Reap on Friday shows Emmanuel Macron and his wife, Brigitte, flanking Cambodia’s King Norodom Sihamoni, as the capital prepares for the Francophone summit. Photograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty Images 
While he is in Manila, US officials will hold a sidelines meeting of the so-called Quad – Australia, India, Japan and the US. In addition, a Francophone summit, which includes the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, is happening concurrently in Cambodia. 
Critical global issues at all these summits will include AI supply chains and governance, tariff reductions and the green energy transition. Trump’s focus has been on denuclearisation. A key regional focus will be on the South China Sea , where Beijing has built massive military outposts in disputed waters, as well as the gigantic Indonesian forest fire haze blanketing the region. 
The humanitarian and security crisis in Myanmar has become a perennial issue, as is status of Taiwan, which China does not recognise. The self-ruled island is sending the founder of the tech hardware company Acer as its envoy to Apec. 
View image in fullscreen 
Passengers arrive at Shenzhen airport ahead of the Apec summit. Photograph: Ng Han Guan/AP 
Global pivots towards Asia
For well over a decade, Washington’s engagement in the region has been coloured by concern over the rise of China, with the then president Barack Obama telling Australia’s parliament in 2011 that the US was “a Pacific power, and we are here to stay” – a policy known as the “pivot to Asia”. 
The strategy of intense diplomacy and trade deals was adopted by Joe Biden, who hoped to gather allies on the continent who wanted to balance their relationships with both superpowers. 
Some analysts see Trump’s transactional style in Asia as a continuation of the pivot policy. Still, the president’s volatility and unpredictability have spooked smaller nations, who regard China as a more predictable partner. 
Jayant Menon, an economist at Singapore’s Iseas-Yusof Ishak Institute, said that countries in south-east Asia had been “laying the groundwork for a future with reduced dependence on the United States” by seeking deals elsewhere, including with each other and the EU. 
“Amid persistent uncertainty and an administration determined to levy tariffs by any legal means, south-east Asia’s ability to ride out another round of tariffs depends on deeper regional integration and diversification beyond the US market,” he wrote this month in the East Asia Forum. 
View image in fullscreen 
Protesters in Manila make their feelings known before the arrival of Donald Trump for the Asean meeting. Photograph: Rolex dela Peña/EPA 
Beijing’s more predictable policies do not necessarily make it any more palatable for its regional neighbours, however, and the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, could have tough talks when he goes to Manila for the Asean summit, especially on the South China Sea. 
China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, recently urged Manila to rein in Filipino politicians who he said had repeatedly “smeared” Beijing, after public outcries in the country over the disputed waters. 
Brunei, China, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam have been locked in decades-long territorial standoffs in the busy waterway, which could sit on deposits of oil and gas . Washington has sent military ships on “freedom of navigation operations”, despite Chinese outcries, although US-linked crises in Iran, Ukraine, Venezuela, and Palestine and Israel have sucked up Washington’s focus under Trump’s second term. 
A decades-long attempt to sign a South China Sea pact is not expected to happen at this year’s Asean summit, as previously hoped. Despite monthly meetings, negotiations will have to continue next year, when Asean’s leadership rotates to Singapore . 
Diplomats at the Asean summit will also be focusing on Myanmar, which is seeking reintegration . Each country in the group is assessing how to deal with their isolated neighbour. The timing of summits this week coincides with a judgment in the international court of justice on Thursday that could find Myanmar responsible for genocide. The coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, remains barred from Asean but is allowed to send a representative. 
Asia’s week of diplomacy will be followed next month by the G20 summit in Miami, Florida, which Xi is expected to attend if US and Chinese relations continue to hold steady.
